notes.meaning: The Lord was angry with Israel for their national sins, so He allowed David to be tempted to take a census of the fighting men. Taking this count sprang from pride and self-reliance rather than trust in God. God used David's sinful desire to bring about a needed correction on the whole nation.

David ordered his general Joab to travel through the entire land, from Dan in the far north to Beersheba in the south, to count the soldiers. David wanted to know the exact size of his army so he could measure his military strength. True security for God's people rests in the Lord, not in the number of troops.

Joab pleaded with the king to reconsider, praying that God would multiply the army a hundred times over. Even Joab, who was usually ruthless, sensed that this proud census would bring trouble and displease God. Sometimes sensible warnings come from unexpected voices, but pride keeps people from listening.

David refused to listen and overruled Joab and his military commanders. The officers had no choice but to obey the royal order and begin the count across the land. When leaders let pride guide their choices, they push past wise counsel to their own harm.

Joab and his officers crossed the Jordan River to begin the census on the eastern side of Israel. They set up their camp at Aroer in the valley of Gad, gathering the local men to be numbered. Starting at the outer borders showed how thorough David wanted the count to be.

The counting team moved northward through the rugged regions of Gilead and newly settled border areas up to Dan-jaan and Sidon. They covered the distant northern frontiers where Israel bordered neighboring nations. No corner of the kingdom was left out of David's military tally.

Next, the officers traveled south along the western coast near the fortress city of Tyre and through towns where Canaanite peoples still lived. Finally, they reached Beersheba at the southern edge of the desert in Judah. Their route took them completely around the borders of the kingdom before turning inward.

The commanders returned to Jerusalem after traveling for nine months and twenty days. It was a long, exhausting assignment that covered every region of the realm. Even so, the huge effort brought grief instead of the glory David had hoped for.

Joab reported the final tally of fighting men fit for military service to the king. The count showed eight hundred thousand warriors in the northern tribes of Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah. Although these figures showed a large and powerful army, trusting in numbers was an offense to God.

As soon as the count was completed, David's conscience struck him with deep guilt. He cried out to the Lord, confessing that he had sinned greatly and acted foolishly. A sensitive conscience is a mercy from God because it leads a sinner back to sincere repentance.

When David woke up the following morning, God gave a message to the prophet Gad, David's trusted seer. Gad was God's appointed messenger who received divine direction for the king. God was ready to address David's wrongdoing, even though David had already confessed his fault.

God instructed Gad to present David with three specific choices for his punishment. David had to pick one penalty, and the Lord would carry it out against the nation. Even in judgment, God showed mercy by dealing with David directly and inviting his submission.

Gad arrived and asked David to choose between three years of famine, three months of running from enemies in war, or three days of deadly plague. The prophet urged the king to think carefully and decide what answer to send back to God. Each option brought serious hardship that exposed the weakness of human strength.

In deep distress, David chose the three days of plague so that he would fall directly into the hands of the Lord. He knew that the Lord is full of great mercy, whereas human enemies show none. In choosing the plague, David and his royal family were just as vulnerable as the poorest citizen.

The Lord sent a severe plague throughout the land from morning until the set time. From Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, seventy thousand people died. The very population David took pride in counting was quickly cut down before his eyes.

When the destroying angel stretched out his hand over Jerusalem to strike it, the Lord showed mercy and stopped the disaster. He commanded the angel to draw back his hand, right beside the open threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. God set His mercy over the city just where the future temple would later be built.

Seeing the angel striking down the people, David pleaded with the Lord for his nation. He confessed that he was the shepherd who had sinned, while the ordinary people were innocent sheep who did not deserve the blow. David asked God to let the punishment fall on him and his own family instead.

That same day, the prophet Gad came to David with fresh instructions from the Lord. He told the king to go up and build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. God graciously provided a way for worship and sacrifice to heal the breach between Himself and the land.

David obeyed immediately and went up to the threshing floor just as the Lord had commanded through Gad. He did not delay or offer excuses after receiving God's word. True repentance always shows itself in prompt obedience to God.

Araunah looked out from his threshing floor and saw King David and his royal servants walking up toward him. He immediately came forward and bowed facedown to the ground to honor the king. Though Araunah was a Jebusite living in conquered territory, he treated David with great respect.

Araunah asked why his lord the king had come to visit him at his threshing floor. David explained that he came to buy the property so he could build an altar to the Lord and stop the plague. Sacrificial worship was needed to turn away God's judgment and bring peace to the people.

Araunah generously urged the king to take whatever he needed for free to make the offering. He offered his own oxen for the sacrifice, along with the wooden threshing sledges and ox yokes to use for fuel on the altar. Araunah was eager to help in any way he could to honor God and stop the suffering.

Araunah offered all these valuable goods to David with the open-handed generosity of a king. He added a heartfelt prayer, asking that the Lord God would favorably accept the king and his worship. His willing spirit showed a genuine desire to see God's favor return to the land.

David refused the free gift, insisting on paying the full price for the property and the animals. He declared that he would not present offerings to the Lord that cost him nothing. David then purchased the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. Real worship requires genuine personal sacrifice rather than shortcuts.

David built an altar there to the Lord and presented burnt offerings for atonement and peace offerings for thanksgiving. The Lord heard David's earnest prayers for the land, and the deadly plague was completely halted. This place of judgment and mercy became the sacred hill where Solomon would later build the temple.
